rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window, reveal critical pairs, and minimize the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to adjust selectivity in either direction.

Lengthen only the gradient to test whether the critical pair responds to reduced slope. The last peak should remain near or below 10 minutes, leaving room to improve resolution without a time penalty.
The critical pair improves with a shallower gradient, but further lengthening risks exceeding 10 minutes. Raise temperature by 5 °C to test selectivity while creating additional time margin.

Return to 40 °C and use a shallower gradient to improve the slope-sensitive critical pair. Raising the starting organic fraction removes early low-organic time, aiming to keep the last peak within 10 minutes despite the longer gradient.
Injection 4 already achieves the maximum CRF and remains the benchmark. Test a higher temperature beyond the apparent critical-pair crossover to seek restored separation with a shorter elution time.

At 55 °C the critical pair appears to have reversed order, so a steeper gradient may now improve its separation. Shorten the gradient by two minutes to test for full resolution with faster elution, retaining injection 4 as the maximum-score benchmark.

Shift the starting organic fraction upward while preserving injection 6's gradient slope and temperature. This should remove low-organic waiting time while approximately preserving the fully resolved pattern; the final organic fraction remains comfortably above the observed elution window.

Make the gradient shallower to recover separation of the new critical pair while retaining the higher starting organic fraction. The 55 °C results suggest the other close pair should remain near baseline resolution, and the last peak should still elute well before 10 minutes.

Several methods already attain the maximum score; now test a substantially cooler temperature for a different selectivity pattern that could support faster gradients. Keep the relatively steep gradient from injection 7 to limit the added retention time.

Test a hotter, higher-organic window to move beyond the selectivity crossover affecting the middle peaks and shorten elution. This exploratory run will also establish whether early-peak compression limits further increases in starting organic fraction.

Lower the starting organic fraction to restore retention and separation of the early peaks, while using a steeper gradient to preserve a short run. At 60 °C, this also tests whether the middle-peak cluster separates on the opposite side of its selectivity crossover.

Shorten only the gradient to test whether the critical middle pair at 60 °C improves with steeper slope after its apparent order reversal. Monitor the neighboring pair, currently at R = 1.62, for compression while seeking full resolution below five minutes.

The steeper 60 °C gradient compressed a neighboring pair before resolving the critical pair. Test a higher starting fraction with a shallower slope to shift middle-peak selectivity while recovering separation, keeping the established maximum-score methods as benchmarks.

Test 30 °C with a shorter gradient to seek a faster fully resolved pattern between the crowded 25 °C result and the successful 40 °C region. The steeper slope may separate a reordered middle pair, while this temperature should improve the near-coeluting early-middle pair seen at 25 °C.

Trim injection 6's gradient endpoint while preserving its starting fraction, slope, and temperature. The last peak previously eluted near 0.57 organic, so an endpoint of 0.65 should preserve full resolution while completing the programmed gradient four minutes earlier.

Shift injection 4's gradient window upward while preserving its slope and temperature to reduce retention time. Check whether the early peaks remain separated and the critical middle pair retains baseline resolution at the higher starting fraction.

Test whether a much steeper gradient at 60 °C separates the middle peaks after their selectivity crossovers, using a low starting fraction to protect early retention. This is a speed-focused exploration; the established fully resolved methods remain the maximum-score benchmarks.

Refine the successful 55 °C region by raising the starting fraction and reducing the slope to compensate for the middle-pair compression seen in injection 7. This tests whether a shifted, narrower window can provide full resolution with greater separation margin while staying below 10 minutes.

Reduce the slope one grid step from injection 18 to improve its sole unresolved pair, while retaining the favorable separation of the other middle peaks. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, offering another route to maximum CRF.

Lower the endpoint one more grid step: the last two runs show steady improvement of the sole unresolved pair as the slope decreases. This should bring that pair above R = 1.5 while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes and the other close pair resolved.

Refine injection 8 with a slightly shallower slope, aiming to increase its minimum resolution while keeping the last peak near eight minutes. This seeks a maximum-score method with more separation margin than the fastest fully resolved run.

Increase the endpoint one grid step from injection 15 to test the speed limit near the fastest fully resolved method. This modestly steeper gradient should shorten elution, with the middle pairs determining whether full resolution survives.

Increase the slope slightly from injection 8, using the 12-minute grid to probe between its fully resolved result and injection 7's faster but unresolved result. This tests whether the last peak can elute sooner while the limiting middle pair remains at R ≥ 1.5.

Use a slope between injections 19 and 20 to shorten the latter's fully resolved separation while retaining some resolution margin. Their local trend predicts both critical pairs above R = 1.5 and the last peak around nine minutes.
